learn.hook: If speed is the derivative of distance, how do you get distance back from speed? Run differentiation in reverse: integrate.
points: Integration reverses differentiation and also measures areas. If F′(x) = f(x), F is an anti-derivative (primitive) of f and ∫f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where C is the constant of integration.
Standard results: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1), ∫(1/x) dx = log|x| + C, ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C, ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/log a + C.
Trig: ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, ∫cos x dx = sin x + C, ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C, ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x + C, ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C, ∫cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C.
Inverse trig: ∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + C, ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C, ∫dx/(x√(x² − 1)) = sec⁻¹x + C.
Properties: ∫[f ± g] dx = ∫f dx ± ∫g dx, ∫kf dx = k∫f dx, and d/dx ∫f(x) dx = f(x). An initial condition fixes C.

example.q: Find f(x) if f′(x) = 3x² + 2x and f(1) = 5.

learn.reallife: From a train's speed log you can recover the distance it covered: integrate speed with respect to time.

games.title: Anti-derivative facts
items: x² + 5 and x² − 3 are both anti-derivatives of 2x.
They differ only by a constant.
The power rule fails at n = −1; ∫(1/x) dx = log|x| + C.
There is no such product rule for integrals.
It is −cos x + C, because d/dx(cos x) = −sin x.

quiz.explain: Integrate term by term: x³ − 2x² + 5x + C.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the new power
Multiplies by the new power instead of dividing

quiz.explain: Split: 2 sec²x − 3 sec x tan x. Integrate: 2 tan x − 3 sec x + C.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the sec x term wrong

quiz.q: f′(x) = 3x² + 2x and f(1) = 5. What is f(2)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to find C from the initial condition

quiz.q: Which function is an anti-derivative of sin 2x?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the coefficient 2

quiz.explain: (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) = x² + x + 1, which integrates to x³/3 + x²/2 + x + C.
quiz.mistake: Tries to integrate the quotient without simplifying

quiz.explain: eˣ(1 + e⁻ˣ) = eˣ + 1, whose integral is eˣ + x + C.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that eˣ · e⁻ˣ = 1

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫(1/x) dx = log|x| + C for x ≠ 0.
Reason (R): The power rule ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C works for n = −1.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is a standard result. R is false: at n = −1 the power rule would divide by zero.
quiz.mistake: Applies the power rule to 1/x

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Why do we always add + C when we integrate?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Constants vanish when you differentiate, so any constant could have been there. + C keeps them all!
teach.nudge: What happens to a constant when you differentiate it?

learn.hook: ∫2x cos(x²) dx looks scary until you spot that 2x is the derivative of x². Substitution is the art of spotting that pair.
points: If the integrand contains g(x) and g′(x), put t = g(x), so dt = g′(x) dx, and integrate in t. Return to x at the end.
∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C.
∫tan x dx = log|sec x| + C, ∫cot x dx = log|sin x| + C.
∫sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x| + C, ∫cosec x dx = log|cosec x − cot x| + C.

steps: Put t = log x, so dt = (1/x) dx.
The integral becomes ∫t² dt = t³/3 + C.

learn.reallife: Physicists simplify radioactive-decay integrals by substituting t = −λx, turning messy exponentials into ∫eᵗ dt.

quiz.explain: Put t = x², dt = 2x dx: ∫cos t dt = sin t + C = sin(x²) + C.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 2x dx is exactly dt

quiz.explain: Put t = 3x + 5, dt = 3 dx: (1/3)∫sin t dt = −(1/3) cos t + C.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 3 instead of dividing

quiz.explain: With t = tan⁻¹ x, dt = dx/(1 + x²), the integral is ∫eᵗ dt.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise 1/(1 + x²) as the derivative of tan⁻¹ x

quiz.explain: The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so it is ∫f′/f = log|f| + C.
quiz.mistake: Misses the f′/f pattern

quiz.explain: tan x = sin x/cos x = −(−sin x)/cos x, so ∫tan x dx = −log|cos x| = log|sec x| + C.
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign and writes log|cos x|

quiz.explain: Put t = cos x, dt = −sin x dx: −∫t² dt = −t³/3 + C.
quiz.mistake: Loses the minus sign from dt = −sin x dx
Forgets the 1/2 from dt = 2x dx

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫cot x dx = log|sin x| + C.
Reason (R): cot x = cos x/sin x and d/dx(sin x) = cos x.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: cot x has the form f′/f with f = sin x, so its integral is log|sin x| + C.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ∫cot x dx needs integration by parts

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I know what to substitute in an integral?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Find a function whose derivative is also sitting there, call it t, change dx to dt, and switch back at the end!
teach.nudge: What clue in the integrand tells you a substitution will work?

learn.hook: ∫sin²x dx has no direct formula. One identity, cos 2x = 1 − 2 sin²x, turns it into a two-second job.
points: Reduce powers: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.
Cubes: sin³x = (3 sin x − sin 3x)/4, cos³x = (3 cos x + cos 3x)/4.
Products to sums: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B); 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A − B); 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B).
tan²x = sec²x − 1 and cot²x = cosec²x − 1.
Odd powers can also be done by substitution, e.g. cos³x = (1 − sin²x) cos x with t = sin x.
learn.reallife: Electrical engineers at power grids average sin²(ωt) over a cycle to compute the RMS value of AC mains (230 V in India); the identity sin² = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 is how.

quiz.explain: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, so the integral is x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C.
quiz.mistake: Treats sin²x like a power of x

quiz.explain: cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, giving x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.
quiz.mistake: Uses the sin² identity by mistake

quiz.explain: tan²x = sec²x − 1, so ∫ = tan x − x + C.
quiz.mistake: Writes tan²x = sec²x + 1

quiz.explain: sin 2x cos 3x = (1/2)(sin 5x − sin x). Integrating: (1/2)(−cos 5x/5 + cos x).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1/2 or the sign of sin(−x)

quiz.explain: sin³x = (3 sin x − sin 3x)/4; integrate each term.
quiz.mistake: Integrates as if sin³x were x³

quiz.explain: cos 2x cos 4x = (1/2)[cos 6x + cos 2x]. Integrate: (1/2)[sin 6x/6 + sin 2x/2] = sin 6x/12 + sin 2x/4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1/2 from the product formula

quiz.explain: (1 − cos 2x)/(1 + cos 2x) = 2 sin²x/(2 cos²x) = tan²x = sec²x − 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses the double angle formulas the wrong way round

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫cos³x dx = sin x − (sin³x)/3 + C.
Reason (R): cos³x = (1 − sin²x) cos x, and t = sin x gives ∫(1 − t²) dt.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With t = sin x, ∫(1 − t²) dt = t − t³/3 + C, which is A.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how an odd power can be reduced by substitution

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'There's no formula for ∫sin²x. How do I integrate it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Use sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, then integrate easily. Identities to the rescue!
teach.nudge: Which double-angle identity lets you lower the power of sin²x?

learn.hook: Six formulas unlock a huge chunk of board questions. Learn their shapes and you will spot them instantly.
points: ∫dx/(x² − a²) = (1/2a) log|(x − a)/(x + a)| + C.
∫dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a) log|(a + x)/(a − x)| + C.
∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C.
∫dx/√(x² − a²) = log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C and ∫dx/√(x² + a²) = log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C.
∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. If the coefficient of x² is not 1, factor it out first (e.g. 9x² + 4 = 9(x² + 4/9)).
learn.reallife: Many formulas in physics and engineering, from orbits to electric circuits, reduce to these standard forms; engineers recognise them the same way you will.

quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1/a
Forgets to take the 2 out of the square root
Uses 1/a instead of 1/(2a), or flips the fraction

quiz.explain: ∫dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a) log|(a + x)/(a − x)| with a = 3.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the x² − a² and a² − x² forms

quiz.explain: The form ∫dx/√(x² + a²) gives log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C.
quiz.mistake: Confuses √(x² + a²) with a² + x² without the root
Forgets to factor out the 9
Forgets either the 1/3 from dt or the 1/2 from the formula

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫dx/√(16 − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/4) + C.
Reason (R): ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = (1/a) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The correct formula is ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C, with no 1/a. So A is true and R is false.
quiz.mistake: Copies the 1/a factor from the tan⁻¹ formula

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I remember which of the six special integrals to use?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Look for a root, then a plus or a minus: no root and plus is tan⁻¹, root over a² − x² is sin⁻¹, the rest are logs!
teach.nudge: What two features of the denominator decide which formula fits?

learn.hook: ∫dx/(x² − 6x + 13) does not match any formula, until you write x² − 6x + 13 = (x − 3)² + 4.
points: For ∫dx/(ax² + bx + c) or ∫dx/√(ax² + bx + c): complete the square, ax² + bx + c = a[(x + b/2a)² ± k²], then use a standard form.
For ∫(px + q)/(ax² + bx + c) dx: write px + q = A·d/dx(ax² + bx + c) + B = A(2ax + b) + B, and find A and B by comparing coefficients.
The A part gives A log|ax² + bx + c|; the B part is a completing-the-square integral.
For ∫(px + q)/√(ax² + bx + c) dx, the A part gives 2A√(ax² + bx + c).
Always factor out the coefficient of x² before completing the square.
learn.reallife: Engineers analysing how a spring or a car's suspension settles meet integrals of 1/(quadratic); completing the square is their first step too.

quiz.mistake: Completes the square incorrectly
Gets the sign inside the square wrong

quiz.q: To find ∫(x + 2)/(2x² + 6x + 5) dx, we write x + 2 = A(4x + 6) + B. What is A?
quiz.explain: Comparing x-coefficients: 4A = 1, so A = 1/4.
quiz.mistake: Compares with 2x² instead of the derivative 4x + 6

quiz.q: For the same split x + 2 = A(4x + 6) + B, what is B?
quiz.explain: Constants: 6A + B = 2 ⇒ 6/4 + B = 2 ⇒ B = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Uses A = 1 or forgets the 6A term

quiz.explain: x² + 4x − 5 = (x + 2)² − 3², so the form ∫dt/√(t² − a²) gives log|t + √(t² − a²)| + C.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin⁻¹ for a t² − a² form

quiz.explain: Put t = x² + x + 1, dt = (2x + 1) dx: ∫t^(−1/2) dt = 2√t + C.
quiz.mistake: Uses the log result meant for f′/f without the square root
Forgets the factor 1/3 or flips the fraction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): To integrate (px + q)/(ax² + bx + c), we write the numerator as A times the derivative of the denominator plus B.
Reason (R): ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The A part becomes an f′/f integral, which R handles directly; that is why we split this way.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why the derivative is chosen

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How do I integrate 1 over a messy quadratic?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Complete the square, shift the variable, and a standard formula finishes it!
teach.nudge: What do you do to the quadratic before using a formula?

learn.hook: 1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) splits into 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2), and each piece is just a log. Breaking fractions apart is the trick.
points: P(x)/Q(x) is proper if deg P < deg Q. If improper, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.
Distinct linear factors: (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b).
Repeated factor: (px² + qx + r)/((x − a)²(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)² + C/(x − b).
Quadratic factor x² + bx + c that does not factor: (px² + qx + r)/((x − a)(x² + bx + c)) = A/(x − a) + (Bx + C)/(x² + bx + c).
Substitute first when needed: with t = sin x or t = eˣ, many trig or exponential integrals become rational functions of t.
learn.reallife: In medicine, the amount of a drug in the blood is often modelled by simple exponential pieces, and partial fractions are one way of splitting a complicated model into those pieces.

games.title: Partial fractions for (3x − 2)/((x + 1)²(x + 3))
items: x = −1 gives B = −5/2; x = −3 gives C = −11/4
Comparing x² terms: A + C = 0, so A = 11/4

quiz.explain: 1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = 1/(x + 1) − 1/(x + 2), which integrates to log|x + 1| − log|x + 2|.
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs of A and B swapped
Substitutes the wrong root

quiz.q: For the same decomposition, what is C?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square (x + 1)

quiz.q: Which partial-fraction form is correct for (x² + 1)/((x − 1)(x² + 4))?
quiz.explain: x² + 4 cannot be factored over reals, so its numerator must be linear, Bx + C.
quiz.mistake: Uses a constant numerator over a quadratic factor

quiz.q: What is the first step for ∫(x² + 1)/(x² − 5x + 6) dx?
options: Divide, since the fraction is improper: 1 + (5x − 5)/(x² − 5x + 6)
quiz.explain: The numerator's degree equals the denominator's, so divide first; then split the proper part.
quiz.mistake: Applies partial fractions to an improper fraction

quiz.q: For ∫x²/((x² + 1)(x² + 4)) dx, put y = x². If y/((y + 1)(y + 4)) = A/(y + 1) + B/(y + 4), what is B?
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip at y = −4
Forgets the 1/a factor in ∫dx/(x² + a²)

quiz.q: What is ∫cos x dx/((1 − sin x)(2 − sin x))?
options: log|(1 − sin x)/(2 − sin x)| + C
log|(2 − sin x)/(1 − sin x)| + C
log|(1 − sin x)(2 − sin x)| + C
quiz.mistake: Forgets that ∫dt/(1 − t) = −log|1 − t|

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I integrate a fraction whose bottom is a product of factors?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Make sure it is proper, split into simple fractions, find the constants, and each piece integrates to a log or tan⁻¹!
teach.nudge: What must you check about the degrees before splitting?

learn.hook: The product rule has a reverse twin. When an integral is a product like x cos x, integration by parts swaps a hard problem for an easy one.
points: ∫u·v dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′ · ∫v dx] dx, where u is the first function and v the second.
Choose the first function by ILATE: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential (earlier in the list = first function).
For ∫log x dx or ∫sin⁻¹x dx, take 1 as the second function.
Results: ∫x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x + C; ∫x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C; ∫log x dx = x log x − x + C.
For ∫eˣ sin x dx, apply parts twice; the original integral reappears, and you solve for it: ∫eˣ sin x dx = (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x) + C.

steps: ∫x cos x dx = x sin x − ∫1 · sin x dx.
example.answer: x sin x + cos x + C

learn.reallife: Signal-processing engineers meet integrals like ∫t e^(−t) sin t dt when analysing radio and radar signals, and they apply integration by parts more than once.

games.title: First function by ILATE
buckets: Take the first factor as u
Take the second factor as u
items: ∫cos x · log x dx (cos x first)

quiz.explain: u = x, v = eˣ: x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the second term wrong

quiz.explain: Take log x as u and 1 as v: x log x − ∫x · (1/x) dx = x log x − x + C.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ∫log x is the derivative 1/x

quiz.explain: u = log x (L before A): (x²/2) log x − ∫(x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2) log x − x²/4 + C.
quiz.mistake: Chooses x as the first function and gets stuck integrating log x

quiz.explain: x sin⁻¹x − ∫x/√(1 − x²) dx, and ∫x/√(1 − x²) dx = −√(1 − x²), so the result is x sin⁻¹x + √(1 − x²) + C.
quiz.mistake: Loses the sign while integrating x/√(1 − x²)

quiz.explain: Parts twice gives I = eˣ sin x − eˣ cos x − I, so 2I = eˣ(sin x − cos x).
quiz.mistake: Stops after one application of parts

quiz.explain: Parts: x²eˣ − 2∫x eˣ dx = x²eˣ − 2eˣ(x − 1) + C = eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + C.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the second application of parts

quiz.q: Which choice of first function is right for ∫x sec²x dx?
options: x, giving x tan x + log|sec x| + C
x, giving x tan x − log|sec x| + C
quiz.explain: A comes before T in ILATE. ∫x sec²x dx = x tan x − ∫tan x dx = x tan x − log|sec x| + C.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of ∫tan x wrong

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In ∫x eˣ dx we take x as the first function.
Reason (R): In ILATE, algebraic functions come before exponential functions.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Differentiating x makes it simpler while eˣ is easy to integrate; ILATE encodes this choice.
quiz.mistake: Chooses eˣ as u because it comes first in the product

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'In integration by parts, which function do I pick first?'
teach.praise: Chirp! ILATE picks the first function: differentiate it, integrate the other. Parts made easy!
teach.nudge: What does each letter of ILATE stand for?

topics.title: Special parts: eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] and √ forms

learn.hook: Some integrals look terrible but collapse in one line, because they are secretly the derivative of eˣ f(x).
points: ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + C, since d/dx[eˣ f(x)] = eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)].
Spot the pair: sin x and cos x, tan⁻¹x and 1/(1 + x²), 1/x and −1/x², x and 1.
∫√(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C.
∫√(x² + a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2) log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C.
∫√(x² − a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2) log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C. For quadratics under a root, complete the square first.

steps: Let f(x) = tan⁻¹x; then f′(x) = 1/(1 + x²).

learn.reallife: Civil engineers find the area of a semicircular arch or gate using ∫√(a² − x²) dx, the formula you learn here.

items.text: ∫√(x² + a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) ___ (a²/2) log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
∫√(x² − a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) ___ (a²/2) log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C

quiz.q: What is ∫eˣ(sin x + cos x) dx?
quiz.explain: With f = sin x, f′ = cos x, the integral is eˣ f(x) + C.
quiz.mistake: Picks cos x as f, but then f′ = −sin x does not match

quiz.explain: f(x) = 1/x has f′(x) = −1/x², so the answer is eˣ/x + C.
quiz.mistake: Chooses −1/x² as f

quiz.explain: (x − 1)/x² = 1/x − 1/x², which is f + f′ with f = 1/x.
quiz.mistake: Does not split the fraction to see the f + f′ pattern
Uses a² instead of a²/2

quiz.explain: Use the √(x² + a²) formula with a = 3; the log term has a plus sign.
quiz.mistake: Uses the minus sign belonging to the √(x² − a²) form

quiz.explain: a² = 16, so the log term is −(16/2) = −8 times log|x + √(x² − 16)|.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve a²

quiz.q: What is ∫eˣ(sec x)(1 + tan x) dx?
options: eˣ sec x tan x + C
quiz.explain: sec x(1 + tan x) = sec x + sec x tan x, and d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x. So f = sec x.
quiz.mistake: Picks tan x as f

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫eˣ(x + 1) dx = x eˣ + C.
Reason (R): d/dx(x eˣ) = eˣ(x + 1).
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: By the product rule, d/dx(x eˣ) = eˣ + x eˣ = eˣ(x + 1). That is the f + f′ pattern with f = x.
quiz.mistake: Integrates x + 1 and eˣ separately

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the eˣ times f plus f-dash shortcut?'
teach.praise: Tweet! If the bracket is f plus its derivative, the answer is just eˣ f(x) + C. One-line integral!
teach.nudge: How do you check that the bracket really is f + f′?

topics.title: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

learn.hook: How much rain fell over a day if you know the rate every hour? Add up rate × time: that is a definite integral, and one theorem makes it easy.
points: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the area under y = f(x) between x = a and x = b, above the x-axis, when f ≥ 0. a and b are the lower and upper limits.
Area function: A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt.
First fundamental theorem: A′(x) = f(x) for continuous f.
Second fundamental theorem: if F′ = f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The constant C cancels, so ignore it.
Definite integral as the limit of a sum is not in the current CBSE syllabus.
learn.reallife: If a rain gauge records the rainfall rate (mm per hour) through the day, the total rainfall for the day is the definite integral of that rate over time.

games.title: Fundamental theorem facts
items: By the first fundamental theorem, A′(x) = f(x).
We must add + C in a definite integral.
It is F(b) − F(a): upper limit minus lower limit.

quiz.mistake: Forgets to integrate the constant 1
Uses −sin x as the anti-derivative

quiz.explain: [tan⁻¹x]₀¹ = π/4 − 0.
quiz.mistake: Confuses tan⁻¹ with log
Subtracts in the wrong order
Forgets that log 1 = 0 and log e = 1

quiz.q: If F(x) = ∫₀ˣ cos t dt, what is F′(π/3)?
quiz.explain: By the first fundamental theorem, F′(x) = cos x, so F′(π/3) = cos(π/3) = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Integrates cos t again instead of using A′(x) = f(x)
Forgets the 1/(2a) factor

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2.
Reason (R): The anti-derivative of sin x is −cos x, so the integral is −cos π + cos 0.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: −cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2. R is the fundamental-theorem calculation behind A.
quiz.mistake: Uses +cos x as the anti-derivative and gets 0

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I evaluate ∫ from a to b without adding up tiny strips?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Find any anti-derivative F, then F(b) − F(a). The fundamental theorem does the strip-adding for you!
teach.nudge: Which limit goes first in the subtraction?

learn.hook: When you substitute in a definite integral, change the limits too. Then you never have to switch back to x.
points: Put t = g(x), dt = g′(x) dx, and change the limits: x = a gives t = g(a), x = b gives t = g(b).
Then ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ from g(a) to g(b) of f(t) dt.
Do not mix: either change limits and stay in t, or go back to x and use the old limits.
∫₀¹ 2x/(1 + x²) dx = log 2 (t = 1 + x², t from 1 to 2).
∫₀¹ tan⁻¹x/(1 + x²) dx = π²/32 (t = tan⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/4).

example.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin x cos x dx.
steps: Put t = sin x, dt = cos x dx.

learn.reallife: Railway engineers converting a curved track's length integral into a simpler one change the variable and limits together, exactly as here.

games.title: Evaluate ∫₀¹ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx
items: Put t = x² + 1, so dt = 2x dx
Change limits: x = 0 → t = 1, x = 1 → t = 2

quiz.explain: t = x² + 1, dt = 2x dx, limits 1 to 2: (1/2)∫₁² dt/t = (1/2) log 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1/2 from dt = 2x dx

quiz.explain: t = tan⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/4: ∫t dt = (π/4)²/2 = π²/32.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve when integrating t

quiz.explain: t = sin⁻¹x, t from 0 to π/2: [t²/2] = π²/8.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the limits

quiz.explain: t = x², dt = 2x dx: (1/2)∫₀¹ eᵗ dt = (e − 1)/2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 1/2

quiz.explain: t = log x, from 0 to 1: ∫₀¹ t dt = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the old limits 1 and e after substituting

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(1 + sin x) dx.
quiz.explain: t = 1 + sin x, from 1 to 2: ∫dt/t = log 2.
quiz.mistake: Loses track of the limits

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x) cos⁵x dx using t = sin x. The resulting t-integral is
quiz.explain: cos⁵x dx = cos⁴x · cos x dx = (1 − t²)² dt, and limits become 0 to 1.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the x-limits after substitution

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): After substituting t = g(x) in ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx, we may evaluate the t-integral using the new limits g(a) and g(b), without returning to x.
Reason (R): As x runs from a to b, t = g(x) runs from g(a) to g(b), and f(g(x)) g′(x) dx becomes f(t) dt.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: R is exactly the substitution rule for definite integrals: the integrand turns into f(t) dt and the limits turn into g(a) and g(b). So A is true and R is its reason.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the old x-limits must be used after substituting

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'When I substitute in a definite integral, what happens to the limits?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Change the limits along with the variable, then finish in t. No need to go back to x!
teach.nudge: If x runs from 0 to 1 and t = x² + 1, where does t run?

topics.title: Properties of definite integrals I and modulus integrals

learn.hook: Some definite integrals that look impossible fall in two lines, not by integrating harder but by using a property cleverly.
points: P0: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt (the variable is a dummy).
P1: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ from b to a of f(x) dx; in particular ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0.
P2: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᶜ f(x) dx + ∫ from c to b of f(x) dx for any c.
P3: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx. Adding the two versions often cancels the hard part.
Modulus: split at the zeros of the expression inside |…| and integrate each piece with the correct sign.

example.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
steps: Write tan x = sin x/cos x: I = ∫√cos x/(√cos x + √sin x) dx.
P3 (a + b = π/2) turns cos ↔ sin: I = ∫√sin x/(√sin x + √cos x) dx.
Add: 2I = ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of 1 dx = π/6.

learn.reallife: A scooter goes forward and then comes back. To find the total distance (not the net displacement), you split the velocity integral where the velocity changes sign, just like a modulus integral.

games.title: Evaluate ∫₀⁴ |x − 1| dx
items: x − 1 = 0 at x = 1, so split at 1

quiz.explain: Sign of x³ − x: + on [−1, 0], − on [0, 1], + on [1, 2]. The pieces are 1/4, 1/4 and 9/4, total 11/4.
quiz.mistake: Integrates x³ − x without splitting and gets 9/4
Ignores the modulus and gets 4

quiz.q: If ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 7 and ∫₀¹ f(x) dx = 2, what is ∫₁³ f(x) dx?
quiz.explain: By P2, ∫₀³ = ∫₀¹ + ∫₁³, so ∫₁³ f = 7 − 2 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Adds the integrals instead of subtracting

quiz.q: If ∫₁⁴ f(x) dx = 6, what is ∫₄¹ f(x) dx?
quiz.explain: Reversing the limits changes the sign (P1).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the order of limits does not matter

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
quiz.explain: Using P3 and adding the two forms, 2I = π/3 − π/6 = π/6, so I = π/12.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve after adding the two integrals

quiz.explain: Split at 5: ∫₂⁵ (5 − x) dx = 9/2 and ∫₅⁸ (x − 5) dx = 9/2. Total 9.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the modulus and gets 0 or a wrong value

quiz.q: Applying P3 to ∫₀² x(2 − x) dx gives which integral?
quiz.explain: P3 replaces x by 0 + 2 − x = 2 − x, turning x(2 − x) into (2 − x)x, the same function.
quiz.mistake: Thinks P3 always changes the integrand

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0 for any integrable f.
Reason (R): ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = −∫ from b to a of f(x) dx.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Put b = a in R: I = −I, so I = 0. R gives A directly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal limits give f(a)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I integrate |x − 1| from 0 to 4?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Split where the inside is zero, use the right sign on each piece, and add. Modulus tamed!
teach.nudge: Where do you split the interval?

topics.title: Properties II: even, odd and classic results

learn.hook: ∫ from −1 to 1 of sin⁵x cos⁴x dx: no integration needed. The answer is 0, and symmetry tells you why.
points: P4: ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx.
P5: ∫₀^(2a) f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx if f(2a − x) = f(x), and = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x).
P6: ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx if f is even (f(−x) = f(x)), and = 0 if f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)).
Classic: ∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿx/(sinⁿx + cosⁿx) dx = π/4 for every n; ∫₀^(π/2) log sin x dx = −(π/2) log 2.
Strategy for any integral: simplify, try substitution, partial fractions, parts, then properties.

steps: Call it I. By P4, replacing x with π/2 − x: I = ∫₀^(π/2) √(cos x)/(√(cos x) + √(sin x)) dx.

learn.reallife: Physicists use symmetry all the time: an odd function integrates to zero over symmetric limits, so whole parts of a long calculation cancel instantly.

quiz.explain: f(−x) = (−sin x)⁵ cos⁴x = −f(x), so f is odd and the integral over [−1, 1] is 0.
quiz.mistake: Tries to integrate directly instead of using odd symmetry

quiz.explain: x² is even: 2∫₀² x² dx = 2 × 8/3 = 16/3.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every integral over symmetric limits is 0

quiz.explain: By P4, it equals ∫₀¹ (1 − x)x⁵ dx = 1/6 − 1/7 = 1/42.
quiz.mistake: Expands (1 − x)⁵ and makes an arithmetic slip

quiz.explain: Adding I with its P4 version gives 2I = π/2, so I = π/4, whatever the power.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve

quiz.explain: cos(2π − x) = cos x gives 2∫₀^π cos⁵x dx, and cos(π − x) = −cos x makes ∫₀^π cos⁵x dx = 0.
quiz.mistake: Applies only the first half of P5

quiz.explain: Adding I with ∫ log cos x and using sin x cos x = (sin 2x)/2 gives 2I = I − (π/2) log 2, so I = −(π/2) log 2.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign wrong; log sin x ≤ 0 on (0, π/2)

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx.
quiz.explain: P4 gives I = π∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx − I, so 2I = π[−tan⁻¹(cos x)]₀^π = π(π/2), and I = π²/4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve after moving I across

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): ∫₋π/2^π/2 sin⁷x dx = 0.
Reason (R): sin⁷x is an odd function.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin⁷(−x) = −sin⁷x, so by P6 the integral over a symmetric interval is 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks odd powers of sin are even functions

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How can an integral be zero without integrating at all?'
teach.praise: Tweet! An odd function over −a to a has equal and opposite areas that cancel to zero. Symmetry is a superpower!
teach.nudge: What kind of function gives zero, and over what kind of limits?
